Question: What is the minimum viable receivables pool size (number of VSLAs / loan count / $ notional) needed to make a securitization economically viable given fixed legal/structuring costs?
Notes: Rule-of-thumb ABS deals need $20-50M+ notional to justify costs; pilot-stage pools (20-50 VSLAs) will be far below this - need a warehousing/aggregation bridge strategy until scale is reached. LIT-012 shows structured funds are more likely than flat funds to reach >=USD 100m, with average fund size ~USD 250m; LIT-011 shows African deals that closed involved large, standardised portfolios with DFI sponsorship. Working target band: private DFI-anchored warehouse in the tens of millions, scaling toward >=USD 100m before public issuance. RT-6 (2026-08-02) adds the OUR-P&L side of the min-pool question: the structuring company's deal-level break-even pool is ~USD 8.6m under likely assumptions (~USD 38m worst, ~USD 3.2m best), complementing RT-5's finding that fixed costs destroy the junior tranche below ~USD 5m and flatten around USD 20-40m. Both point to the same conclusion from opposite sides: pilot pools (20-50 groups) sit 14-50x below break-even, so the DFI-anchored warehousing bridge is the only path, not an optimisation.

Question: Should community receivables (PL-1) and agrivoltaic PPA cash flows (PL-2) be pooled in a single vehicle, or kept in separate homogeneous pools?
Notes: Resolved 2026-08-02: keep SEPARATE homogeneous pools - rating agencies and investors prefer homogeneity, and blending an unproven asset (PL-1) with a legible one (PL-2) risks contaminating the legible line rather than lifting the other; capture the PL-1/PL-2 diversification at the fund/investor level instead of inside one pool. Retained reasoning: The case for blending: the two lines are close to uncorrelated (different obligors, macro exposure and failure modes), which is exactly the diversification the SDS work plan argued for. Neither achieves it alone - PL-2 in particular is only superficially diversified, since many small projects still face one offtaker and one regulator. The case against: investors and rating agencies generally prefer homogeneous pools, and mixing an unproven asset class with a legible one risks contaminating the legible one rather than lifting the other. Likely resolved by structuring advice rather than literature - raise with PT-08 (impact asset managers) and PT-09 (counsel).

Question: Which mechanism actually drives repayment in community-originated lending: information (members' intimate knowledge of each other, enabling screening and monitoring that an outside lender cannot replicate) or social cost (the sanction attached to defaulting on neighbours)? And does that mechanism survive being transformed into a pooled, externally-funded asset?
Notes: Raised 2026-08-06. Partially answered 2026-08-07 by LIT-020, LIT-021 and LIT-022. WHAT THE EVIDENCE NOW ESTABLISHES: the joint-liability CONTRACT is not the active ingredient. LIT-020 converted half of 169 pre-existing group-liability centres in the Philippines to individual liability and found no effect on repayment, with faster growth in centre size; a second trial randomising villages to either regime agreed over two to three years. LIT-021 then isolates a channel that is: first-cycle meeting frequency was randomised and afterwards equalised, so later differences reflect social ties already formed, and monthly-meeting clients were four times more likely to default on their second loan, via improved informal risk-sharing - in INDIVIDUAL-liability groups, with no joint liability present. LIT-022 supplies the taxonomy (screening, peer monitoring, enforcement, reduced audit costs) and shows the information and sanction channels can trade off: 19th-century Irish credit cooperatives failed because members would not sanction neighbours, and the proposed fix of enlarging each cooperative so outsiders could bear the blame 'amounts to throwing away all the information local people have on one another'. SO: the answer leans toward social structure over contract terms, and toward repeat interaction as the mechanism rather than the threat of sanction alone. WHAT REMAINS OPEN, and it is the part that matters most to this venture: none of this literature tests what happens when the creditor stops being the community or the MFI the members meet through and becomes an outside investor. Every study here has the lender embedded in the same social setting as the borrowers. Securitisation removes exactly that. This is the securitisation-specific gap and it is ours to establish, most likely as a pilot design question rather than a literature one. CONSEQUENCES ALREADY ACTIONABLE: (1) RT-2 features should describe group social structure, not liability terms. (2) RT-1 should capture meeting frequency and attendance as first-class origination variables while it is still v0 - see OQ-3. (3) RT-5 correlation assumptions should reflect that repayment is socially mediated within a group. (4) LIT-022 flags a social cost worth carrying into the impact methodology: when a whole group is denied future loans, 'bitterness and recrimination among group members may have far-reaching consequences for village life'. STRUCTURAL RESPONSE PROPOSED 2026-08-07: see OQ-13, which asks whether securitising one level up - lending to the collective, which carries the individual loans - preserves the mechanism this question is about. That is now where the securitisation-specific gap is being worked. CANDIDATE MECHANISM SET WIDENED 2026-08-07. The original framing offered two candidates, information and social cost. Reading LIT-022 in full surfaces at least six more, and the one the strongest evidence actually measures is not either of the original two: (a) INFORMAL RISK-SHARING / MUTUAL INSURANCE - members absorb each other's shocks so a shock does not become a default. This is what LIT-021 measures directly, and it is distinct from both screening and sanction. (b) DYNAMIC INCENTIVES - repayment because continued access depends on it. LIT-022 section 3.4: the threat to cut off all members of a defaulting group from future loans. Requires a lender both WILLING AND ABLE to carry out the threat, which is where it breaks. (c) COSTLY STATE VERIFICATION - the group can distinguish cannot-pay from will-not-pay at low cost where the lender cannot (LIT-022 section 2.3). This is what makes forbearance possible without inviting strategic default, and it is a capability an outside investor simply does not have. (d) ASSORTATIVE MATCHING AT FORMATION - self-selection means safe borrowers group with safe borrowers, screening ex ante rather than by collateral (LIT-022 section 2.1). Distinct from ongoing monitoring. (e) INTERNALLY GENERATED LOSS-ABSORBING CAPITAL - Grameen's Group Fund (compulsory savings, a 5% loan-initiation fee, fines) and Emergency Fund (surcharge on interest) exist to 'make good the loss' when a member defaults (LIT-022). This is first-loss credit enhancement that the community funds itself, which is directly relevant to how a pool would be tranched. (f) SEQUENCED DISBURSEMENT - Grameen lends to two members first and releases further loans only if repayment holds, managing risk through ordering rather than through selection or sanction. (g) INFERRED, NOT EVIDENCED: the group may act as a volatility damper, rescheduling internally so that lumpy individual cash flows arrive as smoother group-level payments. Nothing logged here tests this; flagged as an assumption to verify, not a finding. WHY THIS MATTERS FOR DESIGN: (c) and (e) are the two an external investor most obviously cannot replicate and most obviously benefits from, and (b) is the one most easily destroyed by getting the funding structure wrong - see OQ-13.

Question: Should the securitisation attach one level up - loans to the collective (VSLA/SHG) which then originates and carries the individual loans - rather than to individual receivables? The aim is to keep community risk management intact where it works while using the pool to diversify idiosyncratic individual risk.
Notes: Proposed by BB 2026-08-07, in direct response to the residual on OQ-12: securitisation removes the community as the individual-level creditor, which is the layer the mechanism evidence says is doing the work. Attaching one level up preserves it. THIS STRUCTURE ALREADY EXISTS AT NATIONAL SCALE. India's SHG-Bank Linkage Programme (LIT-023) has run since 1992: banks lend to self-help groups of typically 10-20 women which on-lend to members at rates the group sets. Tankha calls the SHG 'effectively a micro bank as it raises equity and deposits, as well as external funds, and on-lends them'. So the question is not whether the structure works but on what terms it holds up. WHAT THE RECORD SHOWS: NPAs on the bank SHG portfolio were steady at 2.9% in March 2009 and March 2010 then rose to 4.72% by 31 March 2011 (commercial banks near 5%, cooperative banks near 7%). The subsidised SGSY component ran consistently over 5% and above 7% at March 2011. Deterioration is linked to target-driven group formation and to concerns about the quality of groups promoted. The predecessor IRDP programme was wrecked by political loan waivers. RISKS THIS STRUCTURE INTRODUCES, which are different from individual-level securitisation: (1) The group becomes a leveraged intermediary rather than a rotating savings fund. Member defaults aggregate into GROUP default, so idiosyncratic risk is concentrated at the group level by construction before any pooling happens - the diversification has to come from holding many groups, and within-group correlation rises rather than falls. (2) Whose money is at stake changes. LIT-021's mechanism is informal risk-sharing among members whose own savings are lent out. External funds dilute that framing, which is the OQ-12 concern reappearing one level up rather than being solved. (3) The underwriting unit becomes the group as an intermediary - governance, vintage, record-keeping, meeting discipline - not the member. That is an RT-1 and RT-2 change, and it is the same schema deadline flagged on OQ-3. (4) Capital-deployment pressure degrades group quality. If groups are formed to absorb funding, India's experience says credit quality follows formation quality down. (5) Political waiver risk at the group level is systemic within a jurisdiction, so it is NOT diversifiable by pooling more groups in the same country. That is a cross-border argument, and it connects to OQ-1. HISTORICAL CAUTION: the canonical successful joint-liability institution in LIT-022, the German rural credit cooperative, 'financed those loans from local deposits' - it was self-funded, not externally funded. The one structure with the longest success record did not do what we are proposing. NOT YET ESTABLISHED: the securitisation sources we hold (LIT-004, LIT-006, LIT-011) concern MFI-originated portfolios rather than group-intermediated ones, and SHG-BLP lenders were banks with local branch relationships, not remote capital-markets investors. Whether the mechanism survives when the ultimate creditor is an investor two steps removed is not answered by anything logged here. SHARPENED 2026-08-07, and this materially strengthens the caution above. LIT-022 section 3.4 shows the Irish credit cooperatives were not merely a case of members refusing to sanction neighbours. They were EXTERNALLY FUNDED, and in the same shape being proposed here: 'Unlike their German counterparts, the Irish credit cooperatives garnered few deposits. Most of what they lent was a loan to the cooperative from the government.' The failure mechanism was that dynamic incentives collapsed - given the politics, it was not realistic that the government would sue poor farmers, 'making the liability of cooperative members meaningless', and the only real threat available, non-renewal, was exercised only after years of visible trouble. So the German success was deposit-funded and the Irish failure was wholesale-funded, and the difference in funding structure maps onto the difference in outcome. That is the closest historical analogue to a group-level securitisation that the evidence base contains, and it is a failure. The same pattern recurs with a magnitude attached: in Malawi's SACA programme a drought moratorium, plus a rumour that all loans had been extended, saw repayment fall to about 21% (LIT-022 citing Buckley 1996b). DESIGN IMPLICATION, and it is the crux of this question: whoever holds the paper must retain a CREDIBLE AND PROMPTLY EXERCISED renewal decision. A securitisation that disperses the creditor relationship across investors, or that mechanically renews, destroys the mechanism the structure exists to protect. This argues for the servicer keeping a real, fast continuation decision rather than for the pool holding it, and it is testable in a pilot.

The coffee pair's 3.60 composite rests on ASSUMED partner reachability and ASSUMED certification data rails; if LC-24 finds either assumption wrong the cost is a reversal rather than a redirection, so LC-24 moves to the front of the P1 queue. Whichever of the two is chosen must still carry the second randomisation layer (funding source) from research-framework section 3, since that is the design contribution and it needs a field setting. LC-24 READ 2026-08-22, AND THE BET SURVIVES. Both assumptions the coffee choice rested on are now evidenced. Cooperatives do intermediate credit: LIT-031 has Root Capital stating that borrower enterprises on-lend to individual producers, bear the repayment risk, and run origination, disbursement, monitoring and repayment through an internal credit fund - so the cooperative is a lender of record with a portfolio, which is the object of study, not merely a marketing channel. Member registers do work as a sampling frame: LIT-033 compiled the cooperative and certification map from the regional Cooperatives Agency and the Sidama union, then drew 12 certified and 8 noncertified cooperatives at random and 530 households proportional to membership; Sidama alone holds about 57 primary cooperatives and around 85,000 farmers, so the universe is large enough for a clustered design. NO REVERSAL IS REQUIRED. But three things changed and they should govern the pilot. (1) LIT-031 describes internal credit funds as often informal and unregulated, names weak internal controls and accounting as the most commonly observed deficiency, and says credit decisions can be politically or personally motivated - so the data rail must be BUILT and budgeted for, not assumed to exist. (2) Certification cannot carry the welfare claim: LIT-032, a 43-study systematic review that found no RCTs anywhere in this literature, reports price +14% and produce income +11% both significant, but total household income +6% NOT significant and worker wages -13% significantly negative; LIT-034 replicates the household-income null across three continents. Certification organises the population; the outcome has to come from elsewhere. (3) The residual EXP-09 versus EXP-10 choice is unchanged and still sits at M-33, but EXP-09 now has a named comparator - LIT-035 records that Colombia launched a Coffee Price Stabilization Fund in February 2020, which is both a partner opportunity and a displacement risk under OQ-11's logic.

Question: The proposal's stated novelty - that the literature raises but rarely tests loan-insurance bundling - is contradicted by the evidence. Where does the novelty claim move to?
Notes: Raised 2026-08-22 by the LC-04 first pass, which is exactly why that component was read first. WHAT THE EVIDENCE SAYS: bundling has been tested experimentally, at least twice, and both times compulsory bundling suppressed demand. LIT-024 (Gine & Yang 2009, Malawi): rainfall cover required with a seed loan at actuarially fair rates, take-up 13 percentage points lower against a 33.0% uninsured base; the authors attribute it to limited liability already providing implicit insurance, so the premium read as a rate rise. LIT-025 (Banerjee, Duflo & Hornbeck 2014, India): mandatory actuarially fair health cover, 16 percentage point (23 percent) increase in drop-out from microfinance - and this one measures the LENDER's book, which LC-04 had listed as an open question. THE COUNTERWEIGHT: LIT-026 (Karlan et al. 2014, Ghana) finds uninsured risk, not capital, is the binding constraint on farm investment, and demand for index insurance offered SEPARATELY is strong. LIT-027 (Carter, Cheng & Sarris 2016) treats standalone-versus-interlinked as the theoretical question and conditions the answer on risk structure and the collateral environment. SO THE HONEST READING: the contrast is not bundling-good versus bundling-bad, it is offered-separately versus compulsorily-priced-into-the-loan. That distinction is the finding. WHAT THIS COSTS US: EXP-01 as currently written - premium financed into loan principal so cover is automatic rather than opt-in - is precisely the design that failed twice. It cannot be proposed as novel, and should not be proposed at all without addressing why it would go differently. CANDIDATE RELOCATIONS FOR THE NOVELTY CLAIM, none yet chosen: (a) the second randomisation layer on funding source, community capital versus external wholesale capital, which no study in the matrix does (RQ-04, EXP-13); (b) lender-side CASH-FLOW characterisation for securitisation - LIT-025 measured drop-out, not loss curves, correlation or a data tape, and that gap looks real; (c) EXP-17's three-arm separation of the take-up effect from the protection effect, which LIT-024 and LIT-026 together make the obvious next experiment. TO RESOLVE: pick a relocation, then correct the claim in docs/phd/phd-proposal-master.md and the framing in docs/research/research-framework.md section 3. Do not leave the current wording in front of an advisor - a microinsurance economist will know these papers. STRENGTHENED 2026-08-22 by the LC-03 pass, which makes the case against compulsory priced-in cover harder rather than softer. LIT-029 (Annual Review stock-take) states take-up has been disappointingly low WITHOUT LARGE AND SUSTAINED SUBSIDIES - and financing a premium into loan principal is the opposite of a subsidy. LIT-028 (Clarke 2016) shows that with basis risk, optimal demand for an index product is zero for the infinitely risk-averse and nonmonotonic in risk aversion, wealth and price - so low take-up may be RATIONAL, in which case compelling purchase overrides a correct decision rather than fixing a mistake, which is a do-no-harm issue as much as a demand one. LIT-030 measures basis risk directly and finds it and spatiotemporal adverse selection materially drive demand. Taken with LIT-024 and LIT-025, candidate relocation (c) - EXP-17's separation of take-up from protection - now has the strongest literature behind it, and its SUBSIDISED opt-in arm has the strongest prior of the three arms. DECISION 2026-08-22: the relocation is deliberately DEFERRED, not chosen. The four unread P1 components - LC-05, LC-06, LC-07, LC-08 - are to be read first, on the grounds that one of them may move the answer again. LC-08 is the most likely to: LIT-030 already sits there and ties basis risk to the pool's loss distribution, which is candidate relocation (b). CONSEQUENCE, stated plainly: docs/phd/phd-proposal-master.md keeps its CORRECTION PENDING banner and must not go to an advisor until this closes, so there is no proposal-led outreach in the interim. Candidate (c) - EXP-17's separation of the take-up effect from the protection effect - remains the standing front-runner on current evidence and is the default if the four reads do not displace it. Tracked at M-35. BEARS ON THE PENDING CHOICE, from the LC-24 read of 2026-08-22: the coffee setting chosen under OQ-16 turns out to be dominated by TWO covariate shocks, which sharpens candidate relocation (b) considerably. LIT-031 records leaf rust affecting more than half of Central America's total coffee-growing area at once, an estimated 40% cut to Central American output, El Salvador production down 60% in 2013/2014, 40% of Peru's coffee area affected, and 80% production drops at some financed producer organisations in Selva Central. LIT-035 adds the price channel: 45 of 260 reporting days flagged as excessively variable in coffee year 2019/20, roughly one trading day in six. A coffee loan pool is therefore close to a worst case for poolability and, for exactly that reason, the best available case for MEASURING correlation - which is what candidate (b) proposes to do and what EXP-25 tests. This does not decide OQ-17, and it does not displace candidate (c), which still has the strongest direct literature. It does mean the choice between (b) and (c) is now also a choice about whether the anchor's covariate structure is the subject or the obstacle. LC-08 FIRST PASS 2026-08-22 STRENGTHENS CANDIDATE (b) FURTHER, but does not close this question. Two results. First, LIT-038: the standard method for estimating a default probability in a portfolio with no observed defaults - Pluto-Tasche - produces the estimate as an upper confidence bound that is a FUNCTION OF AN ASSET CORRELATION SUPPLIED BY ASSUMPTION. Second, LIT-036 and LIT-037: the historical correlation channel in microfinance is institutional and market-level - concentrated competition, multiple borrowing, social-network contagion, and market penetration above roughly 10 per cent of population - and explicitly NOT the macroeconomy; individual lender growth does not predict deterioration while market-level growth does. Put together, the parameter that does the most work in pricing these cash flows is one that nobody has measured for this asset class, and the obvious way to measure it is not the obvious one, because the channel is institutional rather than environmental. That is candidate (b) with a specific deliverable attached. It still does not beat candidate (c) on directness of literature support, and LC-05, LC-06 and LC-07 remain one anchor deep, so the deferral stands until M-35 completes. LC-07 FIRST PASS 2026-08-22 ADDS A REGULATORY SECOND OPINION TO CANDIDATE (b). LIT-041, the Basel Committee's own validation studies, states that the scarcity of default data is caused by infrequency AND by default correlation, and that correlation BREAKS VALIDATION rather than merely widening estimates - tests assuming independence are so conservative that well-behaved rating systems fail them, while tests modelling correlation detect only obvious miscalibration, so 'statistical tests alone will be insufficient'. LIT-042 (SR 11-7) adds that claimed conservatism must be substantiated and that an extreme point on a misspecified distribution is not conservative at all - which is the Pluto-Tasche bound this project would otherwise lean on. Two independent authorities therefore say the correlation parameter is where the uncertainty concentrates and that no amount of backtesting substitutes for measuring it. That is candidate (b) with regulatory backing rather than only a methodological argument. LC-05 and LC-06 remain one anchor each, so the deferral still stands at M-35 - but the balance between (b) and (c) has moved further toward (b).

Question: Does the multi-originator pool structure diversify on the right axis, given that the historical correlation channel in microfinance is market-level rather than lender-level?
Notes: Raised 2026-08-22 by the theory-of-the-edge section in product-design/business-plan.md, and it is a direct contradiction between the plan and the evidence rather than a new idea. THE PLAN SAYS (business-plan.md section 8, structuring assumptions): 'Originator structure: multi-originator, plausibly regional', sourced to LIT-008 and LIT-011. THE EVIDENCE SAYS: LIT-036 finds four national repayment crises driven by concentrated market competition, multiple borrowing and social-network contagion, with the global recession explicitly rejected as the primary cause; LIT-037 sharpens it to a level-of-analysis result, that individual MFI growth does NOT predict portfolio deterioration while market-level borrower growth above roughly 63 per cent a year and active loans above 10 per cent of population DO. If the operative factor is market penetration, then several lenders inside one market share the thing that actually causes losses, and a regional multi-originator pool may concentrate risk rather than spread it. WHAT TURNS ON IT: whether the first pool can be assembled regionally, which is achievable, or must be multi-market, which is materially harder, slower and more expensive - it multiplies the legal, FX and partner workload. It also bears on the growth model, because at scale in one market the venture becomes the correlation it claims to price. HOW TO RESOLVE: this is exactly what EXP-25's respec is designed to answer - the variance decomposition separates the institutional (market-level) channel from the environmental (agro-climatic) one, and the design deliberately needs at least two lenders per market and at least two markets in order to identify the market level at all. Do not settle this from the literature; the literature is measured at market aggregate and that is precisely the gap. Interim position: treat regional multi-originator as UNPROVEN rather than assumed, and do not build the first structure around it without saying the assumption is untested.

Question: Which operating model does the venture run: the capital-markets structurer in business-plan.md, a solo design-and-arranging practice, or the first converting into the second once there is a track record?
Notes: Raised 2026-09-08. The brief was explicit: drop the PhD for now, design financial products and broker the investor-to-distributor partnerships, stay non-capital-intensive, no hiring. Analysed in full at docs/venture/solo-operator-track.md. THREE OPTIONS, not two. (a) Structurer - the current business-plan.md, highest ceiling, needs capital and a team, slowest to first revenue. (b) Designer-arranger - fastest to revenue, solo-compatible, gives up edge theory 5 (tranching precision) until there is a pool worth an SPV, and requires a research partner to keep theory 2 (parameter monopoly) alive. (c) (b) now, converting to (a) at deal 3-4. THE KEY FINDING is that (b) is not a downgrade of the thesis but the subset of it a solo operator can own: business-plan.md section 5 concluded the stack should be 7 (instrumentation) then 3 (standard-setting) then 5 (tranching precision) with 2 as the research engine, and theories 7, 3 and 6 (verification) all survive intact with no balance sheet, while 5 defers and 2 outsources. TWO STRUCTURAL CONSEQUENCES. First, EU/UK risk retention stops being mandatory because it attaches to sponsoring a securitisation, which removes the only balance-sheet requirement in the current plan - confirm with counsel per OQ-20 before relying on it. Second, RT-5's own sweep says fixed costs dominate below roughly USD 5m of pool and flatten only at USD 20-40m, so a securitisation is arithmetically the wrong deal 1 and the first structure must be a guarantee-wrapped bilateral facility instead. RECOMMENDATION IS (c). What OQ-19 actually has to settle is not the end state - section 4 of the doc is a genuine path from (b) to (a) - but whether to stop paying the PhD's 3-4 year opportunity cost now. Travels with OQ-20 and OQ-21. DETAIL FOR OPTION (c) DRAFTED 2026-09-08 at docs/venture/track-c-plan.md, so the option can be judged rather than taken on trust. It specifies the four things a deferred decision cannot answer: the SEVEN CONVERSION GATES (a contractible pipeline at or above USD 20m per RT-5's fixed-cost sweep; 24 months of clean repayment data originated to RT-1 per LIT-004/LIT-006; an EXP-25 correlation with a usable interval; OQ-18 settled; OQ-1 closed with counsel; the retention capital identified and committed - MEMO-3 does NOT record the required percentage, so get it from counsel; and an anchor investor secured before structuring). The CARRY-FORWARD assets Phase 1 must build for Phase 3, of which data rights is the most consequential and the only irreversible one. The FIVE THINGS Phase 1 must refuse - an engagement-limited data clause, equity in an originator, servicer-of-record status, originator exclusivity, and a securitisation as deal 1. And that STOPPING AT PHASE 2 IS A LEGITIMATE TERMINAL STATE, because if Phase 3 is the only definition of success then Phase 1 becomes a waiting room, which is the likeliest failure mode of (c). Three decision points, not one: D0 now (cheap, reversible), D1 at month 12 (does the cash floor clear), D2 at month 30-36 (convert, against the gates). Gates 3 and 4 can return a permanent no on the evidence, which is the falsification test business-plan.md section 5 already committed to. STEER RECORDED 2026-09-08: PHASE 2 IS THE BASE CASE, NOT A WAYPOINT. Topping out as a design, standard-setting and verification practice is an acceptable end state provided it is a good business in its own right; Phase 3 is an option to be kept open only where keeping it open is free. This narrows OQ-19 considerably - the remaining decision is not which end state but HOW MUCH TO PAY NOW FOR THE PHASE 3 OPTION, and the answer is: only the free things (the data-rights clause, the refinancing right of first refusal, and originating to RT-1 from day one, all of which are good practice for a Phase-2-only business anyway). No SPV counsel, no rating conversations, no retention-capital raise until conversion gate 1 is met unprompted. TWO CONSEQUENCES. First, gate 6 (identify and commit the retention strip) was the one line at which this business stopped being capital-light, and under a Phase-2-terminal plan that line never arrives - THE VENTURE HAS NO CAPITAL REQUIREMENT AT ALL, END TO END. Second, revenue Lane D stops being a year-2 afterthought: Lanes A, B and C are linear in the calendar and bounded by it, so Lane D is the only leg that scales without time and is therefore the difference between a business and a job. Accepting Phase 2 as the end state is therefore also a commitment to PRODUCTISE (OQ-24, M-44), not merely to stay small. Full sequenced decision list at docs/venture/decision-register.md.

Question: What can an unlicensed solo operator be paid for without crossing into regulated arranging or broker-dealer activity, in each market where the practice would work?
Notes: Raised 2026-09-08 alongside OQ-19. Introducing investors to issuers for a fee is a regulated activity in most jurisdictions, and the configuration most likely to be a problem is exactly the one the solo model reaches for: an unlicensed party taking a placement fee from the capital side. THREE WAYS TO STAY CLEAR, in order of preference: (1) bill the originator or the funder for design and advisory work rather than billing the investor for placement - similar economics, different characterisation; (2) take success fees as an uplift on an advisory mandate with the client who engaged you, not as a commission on capital raised; (3) act as an appointed representative of, or co-mandate with, a licensed arranger where (1) and (2) do not work. THIS IS A FIRST-30-DAYS QUESTION because it determines how every engagement letter is written, and it is cheap to answer - a scoping call with the same counsel already needed for the OQ-1 jurisdiction scan (PT-09). Answer it per market, not once: the perimeter differs. If arranging turns out to require a licence in every market that matters, the model is advisory-only and revenue Lane C never opens - which is one of the three named falsifiers of the solo configuration.

Question: Which academic affiliation route supplies the principal-investigator eligibility and ethics approval that dropping the PhD removes, and does it keep a later part-time or by-publication PhD open?
Notes: Raised 2026-09-08 alongside OQ-19. The PhD was buying five things and two of them are not replaceable by effort or credibility: PI eligibility on most research grants, and ethics/IRB approval for evaluations involving human subjects, which a solo company cannot self-approve. Since independent verification is one of the three revenue legs of the solo model (edge theory 6), an institutional research relationship is STRUCTURALLY REQUIRED under that model rather than a nice-to-have. THREE WORKABLE FORMS, detailed in docs/venture/solo-operator-track.md section 7. Form 1, data-brokerage partnership: you broker pseudonymised loan-level access from originator relationships, they bring econometrics, ethics approval and publication - this is EXP-25 and it is the one to start with, because the trade is genuinely two-sided (academics struggle to get lender data, the practice will have it). Form 2, embedded evaluation on a live product with the academic as PI on the grant - IGC is the most solo-compatible entry point, 3ie and J-PAL K-CAI the larger slower versions. Form 3, practitioner affiliation or research fellowship - cheapest route to IRB access, library access and co-author standing, requires no enrolment. RECOMMENDED FRAMING: do not present this as dropping the PhD but as deferring enrolment while keeping the research relationship. It costs nothing to keep open, it changes how academics respond to a first approach, and it preserves a later industrial PhD or PhD-by-publication built on the EXP-25 paper. Approach 4-5 institutions in parallel from day 31 - the MOU takes months and gates nothing else. AUTHORSHIP TERM ADDED 2026-09-08. PI status and FIRST AUTHORSHIP are separate things, and if they are allowed to travel together by default the PhD-by-publication route (docs/phd/phd-by-publication.md) is closed by accident: that route requires lead authorship on most outputs, and a body of work where you are consistently second or third author does not qualify. The research MOU must therefore say in writing, at the start, who is first author on which paper mapped to who does which work - on EXP-25 and EXP-22 the data access, instrument design and costing method are ours while the econometrics and ethics approval are the partner's, so first authorship on those two is a reasonable ask and a far easier one in month 2 than in year 3 - that co-author contribution statements will be provided on request, and that the partner holds PI status and ethics approval explicitly. This is ordinary research-collaboration content that academics negotiate routinely; it only becomes a problem when nobody raises it, which is the default. Form 3 affiliation also does double duty here: several institutions restrict the publication route to staff and alumni, so an affiliate title can be what makes an application admissible at all years later.

Question: Which market does the practice open in, re-taken on commercial rather than research criteria?
Notes: Raised 2026-09-08. Decision D-02 in docs/venture/decision-register.md and the single biggest decision in the work plan - travel is the practice's main variable cost and everything else is downstream. THE COMMERCIAL CRITERIA ARE NOT THE RESEARCH CRITERIA, which is why this is a separate question from OQ-16. The coffee cooperative cluster was chosen partly because LIT-031 makes it the HARDEST CASE FOR POOLABILITY - a research virtue that is close to irrelevant if the practice never assembles a pool, which under the 2026-09-08 steer is the base case. Israel's original justification in business-plan.md section 7 was logistical proximity for a research-first configuration; that is weaker for a fee-earning practice and stronger for cash-flow reasons, so it deserves a fresh look rather than inheritance. SCORE CANDIDATES ON: originators with 10-40 branches (the EXP-22 cluster-count constraint, and a decent proxy for big enough to pay and small enough to decide quickly); a live technical-assistance facility in-market that funds design work, which is revenue Lane B; a regulatory perimeter workable unlicensed (OQ-20); travel cost and time zone sustainable solo; and - ONLY if the EXP-25 research paper is still wanted - two lenders in one market. Note the last criterion is now optional rather than binding, because the correlation estimate has been demoted from a conversion gate to a credibility asset. ANSWERED IN PART 2026-09-09 by the business-scoping pass at docs/venture/market-scan-and-pilots.md, which screened sectors on SIX BUSINESS CRITERIA rather than research ones: is there a financing gap with an identified structural cause; IS THERE AN AGGREGATOR that already holds the relationship and handles money; IS THE CASH FLOW VISIBLE AND ASSIGNABLE; is capital already looking at this sector; does a guarantee or first-loss facility already exist; can one person operate here. THE ORGANISING INSIGHT: follow the visible contractible cash flow, not the neediest population - that is the difference between a structuring business and a charity, and it is the hard filter. RESULT: agricultural value chains with a formal off-taker (coffee, cocoa, dairy, tea, horticulture) LEAD, not because agriculture deserves it most but because it is the only sector where a poor household's income arrives as a documented payment from an identifiable counterparty, and the cooperative or processor's own record IS the receivable. PAYGo solar scores higher on the screen but is the wrong entry point - specialist arrangers already exist and standards have partly settled, so it serves as the comparator that proves the model rather than the market to enter. Urban microenterprise via business associations fails on cash-flow visibility (daily takings are not contractible); housing and WASH fail on both aggregator and cash flow; health and education fee finance fail on capital availability. Migrant-worker finance survives as a niche where Israel proximity is a genuine advantage. GEOGRAPHY: East Africa strongest on cooperative infrastructure, active agri-lending capital and operating guarantee facilities; choose the country by where a first conversation is obtainable rather than by ranking, since the gap between the top three is smaller than the gap between having an introduction and not having one. STILL OPEN: the country itself, pending the verification pass in section 7 of that doc - confirm the guarantee facilities operating there, name 8-10 candidate aggregators and 3-5 active agri lenders, and test the diagnostic offer on three of them.

Question: What is the offer and what does it cost - entry product, fee basis and price level?
Notes: Raised 2026-09-08. Decisions D-05 and D-10 in docs/venture/decision-register.md. Three parts. (1) FEE BASIS - day rate, fixed fee per deliverable, or retainer. Fixed fee per deliverable is usually right for a diagnostic because it prices the outcome rather than the hours, and it stops a solo operator's utilisation problem becoming the client's discount. (2) THE PRICE LEVEL - together with utilisation this decides Phase 1 economics entirely, and NEITHER HAS A BENCHMARK ANYWHERE IN THIS REPO, so both are judgement inputs to be marked ASSUMED in the M-41 model rather than researched. (3) THE ENTRY PRODUCT, which deserves re-examination: solo-operator-track.md section 5.1 proposes selling EXP-22 as the first paid engagement, but EXP-22 is a CLUSTER-RANDOMISED EXPERIMENT requiring branch-level randomisation, timestamped capture logs and HR or staff-representation approval for officer time measurement. That is a research design, and asking a first-time client to host one is a heavy first sale. The alternative is a lighter readiness assessment - the RT-1 field list scored against current capture, a gap list, a costed remediation plan - sold in two to three weeks, with EXP-22 as the upsell. Lighter sells faster and still field-tests the schema, but does NOT produce the per-field cost curve that makes the standard adoptable incrementally, which Lane D needs. LIKELY ANSWER: run the light version two or three times and the full EXP-22 once with a funder paying for it under Lane B.

Question: How is RT-1 monetised - published openly, licensed, or open core with a paid tooling and certification layer - and which paid layer ships first?
Notes: Raised 2026-09-08. Decisions D-16 and D-17, and UNDER THE PHASE-2-TERMINAL STEER THESE ARE THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL DECISIONS IN THE PLAN. Reasoning: revenue Lanes A (diagnostics), B (design mandates) and C (arranging) are all LINEAR IN THE CALENDAR, so at two to three concurrent engagements they are a well-paid job with a hard ceiling. Lane D - published standard, tooling, certification, verification subscriptions - is the only leg that earns without consuming a day. If Phase 3 is not the destination, Lane D is the difference between a business and a job, and these decisions move from month 18 to month 6. THE TENSION: edge theory 3 says PUBLISH, because adoption is the moat, adoption requires giving it away, and business-plan.md section 5 names the falsifier as a DFI, network body or ratings agency publishing a competing standard first - adoption is winner-take-most, so early beats complete. Revenue says LICENSE, because a published standard earns nothing directly. LIKELY RESOLUTION IS OPEN CORE: the schema published free and unencumbered because adoption is the whole point; the tooling (RT-2 scorecard, RT-3 monitor), the CERTIFICATION that an originator's book conforms, and the VERIFICATION ATTESTATION investors rely on as the paid layer. Theory 6 (verification) is what monetises theory 3, and business-plan.md already notes it needs no new capability. D-17 then asks which paid layer ships first - certification is cheapest to stand up and closest to what a diagnostic already produces, arguably just the diagnostic repeated annually under a name that makes the recurrence obvious. Hard to reverse once published, so decide before publishing rather than after.

Question: Which product lines are in scope for the practice's first two years - credit only, credit plus insurance - and does PL-2 survive at all?
Notes: Raised 2026-09-08. Decision D-12 in docs/venture/decision-register.md. INSURANCE requires a licensed risk carrier or parametric underwriter (PT-17 and that whole partner class, which the tracker had nothing in until 2026-09-08) - an extra relationship, an extra regulatory surface and an extra sales cycle for a one-person practice. PL-2 (agrivoltaic project finance) is a further question again: different buyer, 15-25 year tenor, permitting-heavy, and essentially unrelated to the practice's day-to-day work. business-plan.md keeps PL-2 on two arguments - the toolkit is shared, and the two lines are close to uncorrelated - but BOTH ARGUMENTS WEAKEN UNDER A SOLO SERVICES PRACTICE: a shared toolkit does not reduce the sales effort, which is the actual constraint, and portfolio diversification across product lines only pays if you are holding risk, which a fee-earning practice is not. Parking PL-2 for the first two years is legitimate and should be an explicit decision rather than happening by neglect. If parked, mark PL-2's row and doc as parked rather than deleting them - the thesis in business-plan.md section 1 is deliberately layer-agnostic and PL-2 is what demonstrates that.

Question: Is the PhD application track parked while the practice starts, or run in parallel?
Notes: Raised 2026-09-08. Decision D-15 in docs/venture/decision-register.md. M-06 (supervisor outreach), M-11 (first applications) and M-29 (application pack plus a first wave of three approaches) are live milestones competing for exactly the same calendar as outreach wave 1 (M-38). A solo operator running both halves both, and the application track is the one with no revenue attached. THE DECISION IS TO PARK THEM EXPLICITLY - status Blocked rather than Dropped or deleted, so the work already done stays visible and re-entry is cheap - or to keep one narrow thread alive. NOTE THIS IS NOT THE SAME AS CLOSING THE ACADEMIC ROUTE: OQ-21's practitioner affiliation and the authorship terms in the research MOU (D-14) preserve the publication route at near-zero cost, and docs/phd/phd-by-publication.md argues that is the option worth keeping rather than enrolment. Parking the application track and preserving the publication route are consistent positions, and holding both is the recommendation. If parked, also mark OQ-14 and OQ-17 as no longer critical-path - they become research-partner questions rather than proposal blockers.
